headline: Linus Torvalds confirms AI is a useful tool for Linux kernel development
summary: Linus Torvalds, creator of the Linux kernel, has publicly stated that AI is a "clearly useful" tool for development, dismissing anti-LLM sentiment within the community. He emphasized that the Linux project prioritizes technical merit over fear of new tools.
details: Linus Torvalds, the creator and chief maintainer of the Linux kernel, has publicly endorsed AI as a "clearly useful" tool for development. His strong statement came on July 14, 2026, in a Linux kernel mailing list discussion about LLM-based tools for maintainers.

Torvalds firmly dismissed anti-LLM concerns, stating that the Linux project is not anti-AI. He emphasized that decisions are made based on technical merit, not fear of new tools, and that those with issues can "fork it or just walk away."

While acknowledging AI's imperfections, Torvalds argued that its utility is no longer in question. He pointed out that natural intelligence also has its flaws, urging developers to focus on making LLM tools helpful rather than avoiding them.

This project-level signal from Torvalds follows a personal inflection point for many developers, including the author, who noted a significant shift in AI coding tools around December 2025 with models like Claude Opus 4.5.

Initially, AI coding tools required a defensive working pattern with constant review and staging. However, the author found that newer models allowed him to describe desired outcomes, letting the AI plan, write, test, and iterate code.

This shift transformed development from a productivity experiment into a fundamental change, enabling developers to spend more time on architecture and strategic decisions. As one developer put it, running multiple AI agents is like "horizontally scaling yourself."

headline_marked: [[Budget alerts fail to stop runaway LLM spend]], costing thousands, but a fix exists
headline: Budget alerts fail to stop runaway LLM spend, costing thousands, but a fix exists
summary: Budget alerts often backfire due to behavioral psychology, leading to increased consumption, and technical flaws like stale data and race conditions. A new approach with atomic reservations can prevent overspending.
details: An engineer received an 84% budget usage alert but still saw their LLM account burn $1,900 against a $600 cap. This overspend occurred despite the alerting system working exactly as specified, highlighting a deeper issue beyond simple notification failures.

Behavioral psychology explains why: resource depletion alerts often increase perceived value, pulling users to consume the remainder. A 1975 study showed cookies from a near-empty jar were rated higher, an effect not negated by knowing the reason for scarcity.

Technically, budget alerts fail due to lagging ledgers, concurrent processes reading stale numbers, and agent loops outpacing aggregators. This means multiple requests can clear a limit collectively even if no single request overshot it.

The solution is to 'reserve, don't observe,' similar to database transaction management. Using FOR UPDATE serializes concurrent workers, preventing race conditions, and estimating an upper bound for token usage reserves the worst-case cost upfront.

Open-source Python library baar-core implements this with a decorator, raising a 402 error before billing. noburn.dev builds on this for teams, offering pre-flight enforcement, per-user caps, and a ledger view to stop API calls before they incur costs.
caption:
